title: General Chemistry I
description: Chemical structure, stoichiometry, thermochemistry, and equilibrium developed with explicit attention to units, assumptions, and molecular-scale interpretation.

outcomes.description: Balance reactions and quantify limiting reagents.
Relate bonding and molecular geometry to properties.
Use energy conservation and equilibrium models.
Check dimensions and significant figures in calculations.

lesson_objectives.description: Connect electron configuration to periodic trends.
Use Lewis structures and VSEPR as models with defined limits.
Balance chemical equations before converting amounts.
Use limiting-reagent and dilution relationships with units.
Use the first law with a clear sign convention.
Estimate reaction enthalpy from formation enthalpies.
Write a reaction quotient from a balanced equation.
Predict direction of net change by comparing Q and K.
Calculate the mass of solute needed for a target molar concentration and convert between mass and molar concentration units.
Plan single and serial dilutions with C₁V₁ = C₂V₂ and compute the resulting concentrations.
Check a preparation's dimensions, purity correction and propagated uncertainty, and identify the step that dominates the error.
Predict whether a molecule is polar from bond polarity and geometry and relate polarity and hydrogen bonding to solubility.
Use a partition coefficient (an equilibrium constant) to compute how a solute distributes between octanol and water.
Apply energy conservation in a simple calorimeter to obtain an enthalpy of solution, and predict how temperature shifts the dissolution equilibrium.
Account for atomic and ionic electron counts in selected introductory models.
Convert specified entities and synthetic isotope averages with explicit units.
Calculate photon energy and distinguish exact constants from measured precision.
Count valence electrons and formal charges in Lewis structures.
Relate domains, atom shape and bond-vector geometry.
Interpret molecular polarity and interaction-model limits.
Balance equations and calculate limiting stoichiometric extent.
Compute theoretical mass and compare synthetic recovered yield.
Account for remaining ions and final-mixture concentrations.
Calculate gas-state pressure with matching volume and absolute-temperature units.
Calculate mixture fractions and ideal partial pressures.
Interpret kinetic speeds and compressibility under explicit model assumptions.
Apply first-law signs and pressure-volume work.
Calculate reaction heat and molar enthalpy from a stated calorimeter model.
Combine state functions and identify omitted energy terms.
Solve conserved reaction extents with a stipulated equilibrium constant.
Transform quotients and constants consistently with reaction conventions.
Distinguish activity approximations, equilibrium and kinetic claims.
Calculate idealized activity pH and buffer ratios.
Apply neutralization and equilibrium balances before predicting pH.
Diagnose buffer-approximation domains and discriminate calibration/composition explanations.
Summarize synthetic pH reports and correct a supplied reference offset.
Compare nominal buffer ratios with a full ideal mass/charge-balance construction.
Discriminate calibration and composition explanations without unique-cause overclaims.

lessons.title: Atoms, bonding, and molecular shape
lessons.worked_example: For water, two bonds and two lone pairs around oxygen give a bent molecular shape. Polar O–H bonds and the bent geometry produce a net dipole.

lessons.title: Stoichiometry and solution concentration
lessons.worked_example: To prepare 100 mL of 0.20 M NaCl from a 2.0 M stock, use V₁ = C₂V₂/C₁ = 10 mL and dilute to a final volume of 100 mL.

lessons.title: Thermochemistry and state functions
lessons.worked_example: If a reaction's products have a total formation enthalpy of −500 kJ/mol and reactants total −300 kJ/mol, ΔH°rxn = −200 kJ/mol.

lessons.title: Chemical equilibrium
lessons.worked_example: Adding reactant makes Q smaller while K remains fixed at constant temperature; the system then shifts toward products until Q = K.

lessons.title: Making solutions you can trust: mass, molarity, dilution and propagated error
lessons.worked_example: For 500 mL of 150 mM NaCl weigh 0.15 × 0.5 × 58.44 = 4.383 g (4.472 g at 98% purity); 6.0 mL of 5 M stock makes 200 mL of 150 mM; four 1:10 steps take 2.0 mM to 0.20 μM.

modules.title: Polarity, partitioning and heat of solution

lessons.title: Molecular shape, polarity and where a molecule goes: solubility, partitioning and the energy of dissolving
lessons.worked_example: With K_ow = 100, equal volumes leave 0.0099 of the solute in water and 100 mL water with 10 mL octanol leaves 0.0909; dissolving 5.35 g (0.1000 mol) of salt with a -3.3 °C change gives q = -1453 J and ΔH = +14.5 kJ/mol.

lessons.title: Atoms, amount and photon accounting
lessons.worked_example: Take the synthetic 500 nm photon. Convert nanometres to metres before forming hc/λ, producing approximately 3.972892 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Then multiply by the exact amount-count constant and convert J to kJ to obtain 239.253 kJ per mole of photons. Separately, a 0.025 mol entity sample has 1.50553519 × 10²² entities. These two conversions use the same amount-count relation but concern different specified objects. Neither number establishes an absorption probability, measured spectral line or actual sample composition.

lessons.title: Bonding, geometry and molecular properties
lessons.worked_example: For NH₄⁺, start with 8 valence electrons, assign them to four N–H bonds and calculate nitrogen formal charge +1. Four bonding domains give tetrahedral geometry in the simple model. For water, the 8-electron budget instead includes two bonds and two lone pairs, giving bent molecular shape despite tetrahedral domain geometry. Finally, combine two assigned unit dipoles at 104.5° to obtain magnitude 1.224435. Electron budget, atom shape and dipole-vector sum are separate calculations that should agree with their own assumptions.

lessons.title: Reaction extents and solution accounting
lessons.worked_example: For N₂+3H₂→2NH₃, compare extent limits 0.8 and 0.6 mol, choose 0.6 and obtain 1.2 mol product plus 0.2 mol unused nitrogen. Convert product using the supplied 17.0 g/mol to get 20.4 g, then compare synthetic recovery 15.3 g for 75% yield. For the separate ionic example, compare 0.0020 and 0.0015 mol, form 0.0015 mol solid and divide excess 0.0005 mol by the combined 0.250 L to obtain 2 mM. No physical experiment is implied by either calculation.

lessons.title: Gases, mixtures and model deviations
lessons.worked_example: Convert 5 L to 0.005 m³, evaluate PV=nRT and obtain 124.71 kPa. Divide the specified A amount 0.10 mol by total 0.25 mol to obtain mole fraction 0.4, then multiply by total pressure for 49.884 kPa. Independently compare the supplied 135.0 kPa reading to ideal pressure and obtain Z≈1.082512. Finally use M=0.028 kg/mol in the RMS formula for approximately 516.93 m/s. Pressure, composition, deviation and molecular speed are related quantities but answer different questions.

modules.title: Energy signs, Hess' law and calorimeter accounting

lessons.title: Energy signs, Hess' law and calorimeter accounting
lessons.worked_example: The synthetic calorimeter has solution heat capacity 100×4.00=400 J/K plus 20 J/K from the calorimeter. A 3 K rise gives surroundings heat +1260 J, so reaction heat is −1260 J. Divide by 0.0200 mol and convert J to kJ to obtain −63.0 kJ/mol of extent. Separately, add Hess steps −40 and +15 for −25 kJ. In the gas-state comparison, add the positive Δn_gRT correction to ΔU=−10 kJ for ΔH=−5.0116 kJ. These calculations use distinct assumptions even though each tracks energy.

lessons.title: Equilibrium extents, activities and conventions
lessons.worked_example: Start with A=1.0 and B=0.2 mol/L under ideal activity assumptions. Use extent x to preserve A+B=1.2, set the quotient equal to 4 and obtain x=0.76. Check final concentrations 0.24 and 0.96, their ratio 4 and their conserved sum. Reverse the equation for K=0.25 or double it for K=16. For the separate supplied nonideal composition, apply both activity coefficients and obtain Q=1.5. Mixing the ideal and nonideal conventions would compare quantities from different models.

lessons.title: Acid–base buffers and discrepancy checks
lessons.worked_example: Compute nominal initial ratio 0.030/0.050 for pH 4.578151. After 0.010 mol acid, update both inventories before forming 0.020/0.060, yielding 4.322879. At 0.030 mol, reject the zero-base logarithm and solve the weak-acid balance for total concentration 0.16 mol/L instead. For a discrepancy, keep calibration and composition questions separate: a reference constrains reporting bias, while an independently supplied inventory checks the stoichiometric model. Neither step alone establishes every nonideal effect.

modules.title: Virtual lab 1: buffer discrepancy, reference calibration and composition

lessons.title: Virtual lab 1: buffer discrepancy, reference calibration and composition
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic reference identifies an additive pH reporting offset of 0.08. After correcting it, the sample still differs from the nominal buffer prediction because independent composition information supplies less conjugate base. A full ideal mass and charge balance handles the excess-acid condition; no real reagent parameter or unique cause is inferred from pH alone.

grading_policy.attempt_policy: Unlimited formative retries; no summative grade is awarded.
grading_policy.solution_release: Public practice solutions may be shown after an attempt. They are not production exam keys.
grading_policy.late_policy: No deadlines or late penalties exist in this partial package.
grading_policy.appeals: No instructor review workflow is implemented; report ambiguous practice items to repository maintainers.

accessibility.diagram_policy: The seed package contains no imported diagrams; newly authored diagrams require descriptions and individual license tracking.
known_issues: Unicode equations require structured mathematical alternatives and assistive-technology review.

history.summary: Preserved original compact prototype content in separate manifests and readings; labeled partial without semester or credit equivalency.

Added an original lesson on solution preparation (mass and molarity, dilution and serial dilution, purity correction and propagated error) with synthetic data, formative items with computed keys and retrieval cards. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Added an original lesson on molecular polarity, octanol–water partitioning and coffee-cup calorimetry of dissolution with synthetic data, formative items with computed keys and retrieval cards. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Assessments with items now also list the course outcomes those items assess, derived from each item's lesson objective and that objective's outcome links. The rubric-only case lists none, and neither do the 4 prototype-unit assessments, whose objectives are not yet linked to an outcome. No readings, items or keys changed. The syllabus was regenerated from the manifest: it states the current version, lists every lesson with its item and card counts, and describes the current practice and limitations (it still described only the four original units). The course limitations shown to learners were also updated: they still described one formative check per lesson and the original numerical rules. The package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added seven original lessons on atomic/amount/photon accounting, Lewis and geometry models, reaction extent, gases, energy and calorimetry, equilibrium conventions and activities, and buffer discrepancy interpretation; one synthetic calibration/composition buffer lab and a proposed 14-week schedule. Developed with Codex assistance. Two link-only factual references record SI constants and the pH definition, with direct-access limitations stated. Still partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

limitations: Four compact prototype units remain alongside ten original readings including one synthetic-data lab; this is not equivalent to a full university semester.
The proposed 14-week sequence is unmeasured and unreviewed. Graded homework, exams, a laboratory sequence and a cumulative graded project remain absent.
Formative items and provisional objective associations do not establish comprehensive coverage or mastery.
All new amounts, properties, activity coefficients and observations are synthetic teaching examples; no chemical handling procedure, material recommendation or biological conclusion is supplied.
Of 59 numeric items, 12 require units and 6 check specified significant figures; none checks an explicit dimensions field. Other prompts state an output scale and use bare-number tolerances.
CSV summaries and structured choices check selected calculations and interpretations, not written reasoning or causal identification.
SI constants are checked against a primary NIST page. The IUPAC pH definition was verified from its official indexed entry; direct retrieval was blocked and no full-page access is claimed.
Approximation, ideality, stoichiometric completion, fixed-volume and calorimeter assumptions are required; qualified chemical and accessibility review and workload measurement remain outstanding.
intentionally_omitted: Graded assessments, a complete laboratory sequence, a cumulative graded project, measured workload and qualified human review remain outstanding.
